name: Amira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chemistry is a heavy timetable. I have lectures Monday to Wednesday, a lab on Thursday afternoons that always runs over, and problem sheets that take me most of Friday. I live in a flat share with two girls from my course, ten minutes from campus. On Saturdays I work at a garden centre, watering plants and working the till, because I like being outside after a week of fluorescent lights. I don't use AI. I've seen classmates get caught out by answers that sounded right and were wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, quietly. I'd tell my friends that a lot of this was marketing and the useful bits will end up as small features in programs we already use. I wouldn't gloat. I'd just say it was sensible to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plans stay the same, and that suits me. I want a job in a quality lab at a food or materials company, and that still needs a person with a chemistry degree. I'd still worry about a general slowdown, because firms cut graduate hiring when money is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the garden centre job and carry on revising from my own handwritten notes. I'd apply for a summer lab internship, the kind my tutors recommend, and I'd start putting a little by each month. Nothing dramatic, because I don't see a need for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and then a bit guilty for being smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried a chatbot once on a titration question and it gave me a confident answer that was wrong. I tried a chatbot on a chemistry question and it gave me a confident wrong answer, so I check everything myself. That decided it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if prices kept rising for students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and food again. My parents pay for the flat and I cover the rest, but my dad's electrical work can be patchy in winter. If bills jumped, I'd take more garden centre hours and skip the pub nights.

say: I'd say a lot of it was **marketing** and sensible people waited.
I'd tell friends the useful bits will be **small features**.
think: My plan stays the **same**: a quality-control lab job at a food or materials firm.
Firms cut **graduate hiring** when money is tight, and that worries me.
do: Keep the **garden centre** job and revise from handwritten notes.
feel: **Fine**, a bit smug, then a bit guilty about it.
S0.quote: I tried a chatbot on a chemistry question and it gave me a confident wrong answer, so I check everything myself.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to AI comes from a real wrong answer, not from fear.
Calm because her plan and the lab-job route are **unchanged**.
Dry humour, and she admits the **smugness** herself.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the garden centre
Apply for a summer lab internship by February
Put thirty a month into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll have to see how it works in practice. I'd tell my friends that chemists still have to check everything because mistakes cost money and safety. I'd say the people who rush in without checking will get burnt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried. Writing reports, searching papers and planning experiments are all thinking tasks, and those are what junior chemists do. Companies may hire fewer graduates and expect them to use tools I haven't learnt. That makes me uncomfortable, since I'd be behind the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn the tools after all, but slowly. I'd start with the ones my department says are reliable, and use them only for literature searches. I'd also ask my tutor which skills stay important, such as safe lab technique and judging results. And I'd keep the garden centre job as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the pressure to keep up that bothers me, because I like doing things carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which chemistry jobs could change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reports, paper searches, planning the next experiment, and maybe analysing data from the instruments. The hands-on lab work is slower to change, and I'm counting on that. The thinking side of chemistry will go to software first, but someone still has to run the experiment and decide if the result makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide if a tool is good enough to trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check it against something I know. If I can't verify it from a textbook or my own calculation, I don't use it. That's slow, but it's the only way I'd be sure.

say: I'd say chemists must **check everything** because mistakes cost money and safety.
I'd say people who rush in will get **burnt**.
think: Junior chemists do **reports and searches**, which software could take.
I'm afraid I'd be **behind** others who learnt the tools early.
do: Learn the department's approved tools slowly, for **literature searches** only.
Ask my tutor which **skills** stay important.
Keep the garden centre job as a **fallback**.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly about the pressure to keep up.
S1.quote: The thinking side of chemistry will go to software first, but someone still has to run the experiment and decide if the result makes sense.
fieldNote: She is **forced** to learn tools she dislikes, and that is the core of her unease.
Counts on **hands-on** lab work staying human longer.
Her rule, **verify** everything, is her own and consistent.

steps.text: Try the department's approved search tool for literature reviews
Keep the Saturday garden centre shifts as a fallback
Wait a year before changing course or modules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now and not pretend it's fine. I'd say companies shouldn't be allowed to drop people without notice. But I'd also say nobody can truly know what happens, so I'd stay careful about panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very worried. I'd be in the middle of my degree and entry-level lab jobs would be going, if companies don't need as many thinking workers. I'm slow with this technology, and that's not a great thing to be when everything changes in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my tutors about the safest routes, such as lab-based jobs, regulated testing and government labs. I'd look at a master's, since it delays entering the market. I'd also save everything I can and not spend anything extra, and I'd ask my parents to hold off on any big purchases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying awake and trying to make lists. I keep wanting a clear plan and there isn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do to your degree plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd have time to see what really happens before choosing. With two there's no time to watch and wait, which is how I normally do things. My habit is to wait and see, but with two years there is no time to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say stay calm and finish the degree. My dad would say there'll always be work for people who can do things with their hands, and maybe he's right. But my mum would worry in her own quiet way.

say: I'd say governments must **move now** and not pretend it's fine.
I'd say companies shouldn't drop people **without notice**.
think: Entry-level lab jobs could go, and I'm **slow** with technology.
I keep wanting a clear **plan**, and there isn't one.
do: Ask tutors about the safest routes, such as **regulated testing** labs.
Look at a **master's** to delay entering the job market.
S2.quote: My habit is to wait and see, but with two years there is no time to wait and see.
fieldNote: Her **wait and see** habit stops working when time is short.
Looks for **safe routes** through regulated or government labs.
Gets reassurance from her **father's** trade view, but does not fully buy it.

steps.text: Ask tutors which labs hire in regulated testing and government
Look at a one-year chemistry master's to delay job hunting
Save every garden centre wage and buy nothing extra
Skip nights out and cut my takeaway budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time, if people use it well. I'd tell my friends to keep up with the science and not to follow the hype. And I'd say employers should say plainly what they plan to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel a bit better. I'd graduate in 2029, maybe do a master's, and get at least a couple of years in the lab before 2031. The robots by 2034 are a worry for lab technicians, but I'd hope to be a scientist who uses them, not a technician they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take the internship, and learn the lab software in third year when I'm more confident. I'd save about two thousand a year so I'd have a cushion. And I'd look for companies in regulated industries like pharmaceuticals, which move slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy again, but manageable. It's like waiting for a big exam: you can prepare, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time lets me do the master's and get experience before the full change. Five years lets me do the master's and learn the tools in my own time, so I'd be ready and not rushed. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a sign to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If job adverts for graduate chemists dropped sharply, or if my university cut places, I'd take that as the sign. I'd also watch what my tutors do, since they'd see it before I would.

say: I'd say five years is **decent time** if people use it well.
I'd tell friends not to follow the **hype**.
think: I'd get a couple of **lab years** in before 2031.
I hope to use robots as a scientist, not be replaced as a **technician**.
do: Finish the degree and take a **summer internship**.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, like waiting for a big exam.
S3.quote: Five years lets me do the master's and learn the tools in my own time, so I'd be ready and not rushed.
fieldNote: The **extra time** is what allows her slow, careful way of learning.
Plans around **regulated** industries because they move slowly.
Uses **exam** language, so she treats the future as something to revise for.

steps.text: Do a master's in analytical chemistry after the degree
Save two thousand a year from the garden centre and my parents
Learn the lab software in third year, once confident

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time and we should be careful and sensible. I'd tell people not to throw their degrees away or rush into things. And I'd say schools should keep teaching the basics, like how to check a result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd relax a lot. I'd have nearly a decade as a chemist, perhaps even a chartered one, before 2036. Robots arrive around 2039, when I'd be thirty, and by then I'd hope to be in a senior or supervising job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, a master's, and take a graduate scheme. I'd learn tools once they've proven themselves, as I always do. I'd save for a flat deposit, and keep the garden centre job in the holidays while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Ten years feels like normal life with a bit of background noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you stop worrying about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying about whether my degree is a waste. Ten years is long enough for a whole career, so my degree isn't wasted, and that's the thing I was most afraid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays on your mind anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents getting older, to be honest. In ten years my dad won't want to climb ladders and fit cables, and I'd want to help them without being stuck.

say: I'd say we should be **careful and sensible** and not rush.
I'd say schools should keep teaching how to **check a result**.
think: I'd have nearly **a decade** as a chemist, maybe chartered, before AGI.
By 2039 I'd hope to be in a **supervising** job.
do: Do the degree, a **master's** and a graduate scheme.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a whole career, so my degree isn't wasted, and that's the thing I was most afraid of.
fieldNote: With a **decade**, the question moves from her job to her **parents'** later years.
Keeps her habit of adopting tools only once **proven**.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply to graduate schemes in chemistry
Complete a master's in analytical chemistry
Save for a flat deposit over the next six years
Plan time and money to help my dad when he stops fitting cables

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My normal habit is to wait and watch, and that doesn't work when everything happens fast. What would help is a clear plan from employers and government, written down, plus a guarantee that graduate lab jobs won't disappear overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology, I'm just careful with it. I'd like someone to show me which tools are safe and reliable so I can use them without feeling reckless.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology, I'm just careful with it.
portrait: Amira is a 19-year-old **chemistry** student who works at a garden centre and never uses AI tools.
A chatbot once gave her a confident wrong answer, and she now checks **everything** herself.
Her dad is an electrician and her mum does school admin part-time, and she worries about their future.
She is calm when little changes, **anxious** in the two-year world, and eases with ten years.
She wants safe routes: a master's, regulated labs and tools only once they are proven.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world, because her habit of waiting and watching would not work.
whatWouldHelp: A clear written **plan** from employers and government.
A **guarantee** that graduate lab jobs won't vanish overnight, and a list of reliable tools.
